Article Title: Historic medal for India! Wrestler Vishvajit More clinches first-ever Greco-Roman silver at U23 Worlds
Article Text:
Vishvajit More (SAI Photo)

More’s impressive run to the final

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Visa rejections hit India’s campaign

Indian wrestler Vishvajit Ramchandra More made history by winning silver in the men’s 55kg Greco-Roman category at the U23 World Wrestling Championships in Las Vegas on Thursday.He narrowly lost 12-13 to Georgia’s Koba Karumidze in the final seconds of the gold medal bout, becoming the first Indian to win silver in Greco-Roman wrestling at the U23 World Championships.More had previously won two bronze medals at the same competition, making him India’s only Greco-Roman wrestler to secure two medals at the U23 Worlds. He also became the first Indian wrestler to reach the final in this category on Tuesday.The Indian wrestler secured three hard-fought victories to reach the final. He began with a 10-8 win over Mexico’s Isaac Marin Mata before defeating Iran’s U20 world champion Armin Shamsipour 8-1 in the quarterfinals with a four-point throw.In the semifinal, More beat Russia’s Malik Gigiev 6-4 in another closely contested match. He then aimed to become India’s first Greco-Roman gold medallist at the U23 World Championships but fell just short against Karumidze.India’s overall campaign also faced a setback after nine wrestlers across the Greco-Roman and women’s categories were denied US visas. The wrestlers were reportedly rejected because they were under 20 and did not have full-time jobs.Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) chief Sanjay Singh criticised the decision, claiming it affected India’s medal chances."The US Embassy rejected the visas of nine Indian wrestlers on the grounds that they are unemployed. For the first time in history this has happened. Even the UWW president wrote to them regarding the matter. This visa refusal is entirely the US Embassy's fault, and as a result, India lost out on gold medals. Among the nine wrestlers denied visas, at least two were strong gold medal prospects. India suffered a major medal loss due to the US Embassy's fault," WFI chief Sanjay Singh told news agency IANS on Wednesday
Article Summary: Vishvajit Ramchandra More made history by winning silver in the men’s 55kg Greco-Roman category at the U23 World Wrestling Championships in Las Vegas. He narrowly lost 12-13 to Georgia's Koba Karumidze in the final seconds of the gold medal bout. More had previously won two bronze medals at the same competition. He also became the first Indian wrestler to reach the final in this category.

Article Title: BCCI steps in to save Arunachal's domestic season
Article Text:
Image credit: X

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

MUMBAI: With Arunachal Pradesh forfeiting its Ranji Trophy opener against Nagaland and missing participation in two age-group tournaments, the BCCI has moved swiftly to ensure the state’s cricketers do not suffer further more of the administrative logjam.The board has constituted a three-member selection committee to pick Arunachal Pradesh’s men’s and women’s teams across age groups, paving the way for the state to continue its participation in the domestic season. This is despite a legal battle within Arunachal Cricket Association (ACA).The move follows Arunachal’s forfeiture of its opening Ranji Trophy fixture in Ahmedabad after the association failed to field a team. The state also missed Vinoo Mankad Trophy and Under-19 Women’s T20 Trophy as rival ACA factions remain embroiled in litigation before Itanagar Bench of Guwahati High Court.Thanks to BCCI’s intervention, however, Arunachal Pradesh is now expected to take the field for its next Ranji Trophy match against Sikkim in Nadiad from Oct 18.BCCI apex council member M Khairul Jamal Majumdar has been appointed convener of the arrangement.The selection panel consists of former Assam cricketers Satya Gopal Chakraborty, Jayanta Chowdhury and Deep Bora, with Chakraborty serving as chairman.The committee has been tasked with conducting trials and selecting teams for Ranji Trophy, Col CK Nayudu Trophy, Senior Women’s T20 Trophy and Vijay Merchant Trophy.Explaining the board’s decision, BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia said protecting players’ interests had been the overriding priority.“We have made our apex council member Khairul Mamun Mazumdar the convener and appointed three selectors who have been conducting the entire process over the last three days. The BCCI wants to ensure that no player is denied opportunities because of circumstances beyond their control. We have a robust domestic structure and every player deserves a chance to showcase his or her talent,” Saikia told TOI on Wednesday.Drawing parallels with a similar situation in Bihar in the past, Saikia said the board had adopted the same approach by appointing an independent mechanism to keep cricketing activities on track.
Article Summary: Arunachal Pradesh forfeited its Ranji Trophy opener against Nagaland. The state also missed participation in two age-group tournaments. The BCCI has constituted a three-member selection committee. This is despite a legal battle within ArunachAl Cricket Association (ACA)

Article Title: Ranji Trophy: Bengal hand Delhi defeat in opener
Article Text:

KALYANI: Bengal coach Laxmi Ratan Shukla exuded quiet confidence at the end of Day Three on Tuesday, when Delhi needed 88 runs more with seven wickets in hand to make the hosts bat again, with the hope of preventing them from recording an outright win.The bowlers did live up to the challenge as Bengal made a winning start to their Ranji campaign, beating Delhi by nine wickets in their Elite Group ‘C’ clash at the Bengal Cricket Academy (BCA) ground here on Wednesday.While Bengal ended with six points, Delhi have plenty to ponder as they returned empty-handed. However, the hosts were guilty of missing out on bagging maximum points (7), as they lost opener Ankur Paul caught by Dev Lakra off Hrithik Shokeen while going for a big shot in the 89-run victory chase.On a day when seven wickets fell to spin, it was the lesser known Sumanta Gupta who made the difference.Delhi made a good start on the last day with Ayush Badoni and Anuj Rawat managing to see off the tricky first hour. Bengal tasted first blood when Rawat was clean bowled attempting a rather unnecessary reverse sweep off Aamir Gani to be clean bowled.But, Yash Dhull, who retired hurt last evening, came out to give his skipper good support as the duo started to rebuild the innings.Easwaran then threw the ball to Gupta for the last over before lunch and the part-time off-spinner provided the much-needed breakthrough with his second delivery of the match. Dhull stretched forward as the ball bounced up hitting the pad and then kissed his gloves to land into the safe hands of wicketkeeper Abishek Porel.The opener felt not allowing the Delhi batters to score freely kept Bengal in the match.Delhi suffered the greatest jolt when left-arm spinner Pradipta Pramanik got in-form Badoni (85) caught at first slip by Easwaran.Like the first innings, the Delhi tail did put up some resistance before folding up for 277 in the extended second session before the tea interval.Both Easwaran and Paul ensured smooth going. After Paul’s departure for 38, Easwaran (34*) and Sudip Gharami (16*) took the side home in 15.3 overs.
Article Summary: Bengal beat Delhi by nine wickets in their Elite Group ‘C’ clash at the Bengal Cricket Academy (BCA) ground here on Wednesday. Delhi lost opener Ankur Paul caught by Dev Lakra while going for a big shot in the 89-run victory chase.

Article Title: Rory McIlroy’s encore, Tommy Fleetwood’s own opera: Golf’s big stage awaits
Article Text:
Rory McIlroy

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Race To Dubai leader Patrick Reed saw a monkey running across the fairway at No. 13. “Never seen that,” he said, grinning after the Wednesday Pro-Am outing at the India Championship.The teeming wildlife at Delhi Golf Club was there to keep him company, because for all the kids and their parents, all roads lead to the 18th, where Rory McIlroy’s bobbing figure emerged. The six-time Major winner broke into childlike laughter, clearly enjoying the day as he glowed in the afternoon sun.The round done, everyone was scrambling to get a piece of the World No. 2. Left profile, right, front, selfies clicked, and caps signed until he was whisked away in a buggy.The serious stuff begins on Thursday. There is a tournament to be won, and the race is on as the golfers see the $4 million WIC as an approach shot to the business end of the ‘Back 9’ series.The goalposts change. Rory, whose childhood dream was to “win all four Majors and be the best in the world” has ticked his boxes. Now, the focus is on equalling Colin Montgomerie’s record of claiming eight European Order of Merit titles.“Eugenio (Chacarra) jumped over me to second place last week in Spain. With Patrick missing the cut last week, I think this is really a good opportunity this week to cut into that lead and head to the Middle East in a really good spot.”Eye on the prize for now, but there’s plenty ahead for the 37-yearold who seemed to have conquered all his demons, having won the Masters twice in a row “Obviously the Majors will always be important. I want to make the Ryder Cup team.”“A lot of plates spinning,” the global golfer admitted. “There’s international golf, but obviously the bulk of my play is in America.”With his stature, comes a lot of responsibility too. Taking time out to meet Asian Games women’s golf gold medallist Pranavi Urs, who had said Rory’s resilience inspired her in Japan, was his pleasure.But if one was a junior golfer visiting DGC this week, who should they watch? He points to others. “If it’s a golfer’s prep, practice, diligence, work ethic, everything that he does off the course, it would be Aaron Rai,” he spoke glowingly of the PGA Championship winner.And then there’s Tommy Fleetwood, the defending champion, with whom he will be teeing off in the morning. “I always love watching Tommy hit balls in practice.”Sweet, mild-mannered Tommy had conducted his own rock opera in his hometown of Southport during this year’s Open Championship. “I was achieving a dream that I had as a seven-year-old boy at that very golf course. It was like having your own concert,” said the man from the Liverpool suburbs, who had finished tied-4th.It did not reach that crescendo, but he will always be grateful. “Not everybody gets those moments and those experiences.”Last year, he celebrated on the closing greens of DGC with his son Frankie, another emotional high. The eight-year-old is here. Will he be the good luck charm again?
Article Summary: Rory McIlroy is playing in the Race To Dubai at the India Championship. The World No. 2 is looking to equal Colin Montgomerie's record of eight European Order of Merit titles. The Northern Irishman will be teeing off in the morning with defending champion Tommy Fleetwood.

Article Title: Ryan Fox, Min Woo Lee brace for unique DGC test
Article Text:
Ryan Fox (Image credit: X)

NEW DELHI: The Delhi Golf Club is a course that demands patience, imagination and acceptance that power alone will not guarantee success. For Ryan Fox and Min Woo Lee, two of the most recognisable names in the field at the India Championship, the challenge begins with leaving one of their biggest weapons out of the bag: the driver.Ahead of the tournament, both players offered an insight into the demands of a venue where narrow fairways, dense rough and intricate greens are expected to reward discipline over aggression. For Fox, arriving in India after a career-defining victory at The Open Championship at the Royal Birkdale earlier this year, the change represents an intriguing tactical challenge. For Lee, it is another opportunity to test the progress he has made in developing a more complete game.“Very unique. No drivers, which is a little bit different to a normal course,” Lee said of the course after playing the Pro-Am. “It’s going to test my mental strength this week,” he added.The Australian expects the conditions to make life particularly difficult for those who stray from the fairway.Meanwhile, Fox arrives in the Capital with a different perspective on pressure. The New Zealander admitted that winning a Major has changed almost every aspect of his professional life and bringing greater attention.The biggest adjustment has been learning when to say no and protecting the time needed to prepare.Lee has built his reputation on prodigious hitting, an entertaining personality and an attacking style. However, his preparations for the new season have involved a significant technical transformation.The Australian revealed that he initially resisted changes suggested by his coaching team, believing his explosive swing remained good enough. Eventually, however, he accepted that further progress required a willingness to rebuild.“We probably did a whole month of boot camp, like not even seeing a golf ball,” Lee said.
Article Summary: Ryan Fox and Min Woo Lee are in India to compete in the India Championship. Fox won The Open Championship at the Royal Birkdale earlier this year. Lee says the Delhi Golf Club course is'very unique' and will 'test my mental strength'

Article Title: ISL: Raphael Eric Messi Bouli's late winner helps Punjab FC beat Odisha in thriller

Article Title: From introduction to skeet gun at 13 to Asian Games bronze: Parinaaz Dhaliwal’s journey of precision, perseverance and the right support
Article Text:
Parinaaz Dhaliwal

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: For Parinaaz Dhaliwal, success in skeet shooting is about much more than hitting targets. It is a combination of technical precision, mental strength, financial backing and the ability to find balance under pressure. After years of investing in her game, the Asian Games medallist believes experience, the right coaching environment and an unwavering support system have helped her take significant strides forward.When Parinaaz looks back at her journey in shooting, she does not attribute her progress to one competition, one coach or one breakthrough moment. Instead, she sees it as an evolution shaped by years of training, international exposure and lessons learnt along the way. The bronze medal in the women’s skeet team event at the Asian Games 2026 at Aichi-Nagoya in Japan alongside Raiza Dhillon and Maheshwari Chauhan, was a significant milestone in that journey.“It was bits of everything, to be honest,” she says, reflecting on the difference between her previous Asian Games appearance and the latest campaign. “You evolve with every single competition. You learn something or the other.You win or you don’t win, but you always learn.”The medal was the culmination of a more comprehensive preparation programme, one that she believes made a tangible difference. Ahead of the Games, the Sports Authority of India (SAI), in coordination with the National Rifle Association of India (NRAI), organised two preparatory camps. The first, held in Aug, focused on fundamentals, while the Sept camp concentrated on fine-tuning and final preparations.The support structure, she says, was also stronger than before, with foreign coaching expertise and a larger team of support staff contributing to the preparations.An important part of that preparation was the presence of her personal coach, Anthony, an Olympic medallist from France. She received permission from the federation to have him join the national camp and accompany her to Japan, where he worked alongside national coaches and foreign coach Riccardo Filippelli.For her, the arrangement was about more than technical advice. A personal coach who has worked with an athlete over an extended period understands the individual beyond the shooting range, including their habits, temperament and response to pressure.“My personal coach might have seen my tantrums or might have seen a lot,” she says with a laugh. “He has seen various sides of me because I train with him a lot more than I do with my national coach.”She is particularly appreciative of the cooperation between the coaches, describing the atmosphere as one without ego or insecurity. Anthony, she adds, was equally conscious of respecting the national coaching structure.Her introduction to shooting began well before she took up skeet seriously. Growing up around firearms, she was familiar with the sport, and her father, Ratandeep Dhaliwal, encouraged her to learn how to use a weapon. At Mayo College Girls’ School in Ajmer, she participated in open-sight shooting competitions and school-level events.When she turned 13, her father suggested that she explore shotgun shooting. She initially tried trap, but it was an unexpected session at the skeet range that changed her trajectory.During a week at home to prepare for a state competition, her mentor, Amarjang Singh Sidhu, suggested that she try a station of skeet. She hit a couple of targets and immediately found herself drawn to the discipline.“I looked at my dad and said, ‘Papa, I think I want to do skeet.’ He was like, ‘Huh?’” she recalls.Her father discussed the decision with her grandfather, and by the following day, she had a skeet gun.“It turned out to be a great decision,” she says. While she remains close to several trap shooters, skeet is the discipline she finds more engaging. The experience reinforced a lesson she considers fundamental to sporting success: an athlete must enjoy what they do.Behind the medals, however, lies a challenge that is often overlooked: the financial demands of competitive shooting.Shotgun shooting, she explains, can be particularly expensive, making financial stability and institutional support crucial for aspiring athletes. Equipment, training and travel can place a substantial burden on families, while sponsorships often arrive only after an athlete has established a record.Despite having competed at the previous Asian Games, she says she relied on her family to fund her development for years, even while working with internationally accomplished coaches, fitness professionals and sports psychologists.She is grateful for the backing, but is equally conscious of the sacrifices that preceded it. Her father had travelled with her to competitions and camps, both in India and abroad. This year, however, he stepped back from travelling because her grandparents were unwell and needed family support.“I said, for me and for my mental sanity, it’s just better that you are at home with my grandparents. And I’m fine,” she says, drawing on the independence she developed during her years at boarding school.For young shooters, she believes, understanding the financial realities of the sport is as important as recognising their own potential.Parinaaz’s preparation has evolved beyond technique and equipment. Over the past three years, she has worked extensively on fitness and the technical aspects of her shooting, while also consulting a sports psychologist based in the UK.At the elite level, she believes, every component matters. “You cannot leave anything unattended at all,” she said.One incident from the World Cup in Lonato, Italy, illustrates the importance she places on mental preparation. After the first four rounds, she was uncertain about her standing and found herself worrying about the competition. Anthony responded by taking her out for dinner rather than allowing her anxiety to dominate the evening.She was initially concerned about losing sleep ahead of the following morning’s round. Her coach, however, believed that continuing to dwell on the competition would be counterproductive.The evening continued with a walk by the lake and gelato, helping her shift her attention away from the scoreboard and reconnect with the reasons she had taken up shooting.Anthony, she said, believes strongly in maintaining balance and reminding athletes why they compete in the first place.The next day, she shot a perfect round of 25, her best of the competition, which helped her reach a shoot-off.“These are the small things that coaches with experience can teach you,” she said.At the Asian Games, the women's team faced a difficult opening day, but the athletes concentrated on their individual routines rather than becoming distracted by the collective result.Skeet may have a team component, but the discipline demands individual accountability. Each shooter must execute their own process, manage pressure and remain focused on the target in front of them.The team's positive atmosphere helped them persevere, while the men's skeet team also produced a strong finish. India ultimately returned with medals in both the men's and women's team events.For her, the result reflected not only individual ability but also the value of a supportive environment in which athletes and coaches worked towards a common objective.She also believes India's development in skeet coaching needs greater attention. While the country has several accomplished coaches in trap, she sees a relative shortage of experienced specialists in skeet. International coaches, despite their high fees, can offer technical knowledge and an understanding of competitive pressure acquired through years at the highest level.At the same time, she acknowledges that being an accomplished shooter does not automatically make someone an accomplished coach. Coaching, she says, is a discipline in itself.Looking ahead, she intends to continue building on the progress she has made through competition experience, technical refinement and mental preparation. Her latest Asian Games performance is a milestone, but not the end of the journey.For a shooter whose career began with a spontaneous decision at 13, the larger lesson remains remarkably simple: excellence comes from getting the fundamentals right, learning from every competition and finding the people who help you become better.And perhaps that is what defines Parinaaz’s journey best. The targets may be fleeting, but the work behind each shot is anything but.
Article Summary: Parinaaz Dhaliwal won a bronze medal in the women's skeet team event at the Asian Games 2026 at Aichi-Nagoya in Japan. She believes experience, the right coaching environment and an unwavering support system have helped her take significant strides forward. She is grateful for the backing, but equally conscious of the sacrifices that preceded it.

NEW DELHI: In May 2019, before the pandemic had pressed the pause button on the world, Sagar Shah, already an International Master (IM) and one of the most influential voices in today's chess fraternity, wrote a line in his ChessBase column: "Just like Humpy (Koneru) and Harika (Dronavalli) have made the world take note of Indian women's chess over the years, we have a feeling that within a few years Sahithi (Varshini Moogi) and Savitha (Shri Baskar) will also be right up there with the best in women's chess!"More than seven years have passed, and the same line reads less like a prediction and more like a question of legacy, much like asking whether Lamine Yamal could become the next Lionel Messi for Barcelona or whether Carlos Alcaraz could carry the torch of Spanish tennis after Rafael Nadal.Both girls are now 19. At the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand last month, Savitha added a team bronze to her growing list of accolades while also becoming the only Indian to win an individual gold medal at the event Sahithi Varshini, on the other hand, has had a less decorated career so far. The Vizag-born prodigy recently became India’s latest Woman Grandmaster (WGM), a milestone by any measure. But is this the best she can do?"Whatever she has achieved so far, including this one (the WGM title), is not up to her potential. This is just a mere beginning," Lokeswara Moogi Rao, her father and only coach to date, told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interaction.Just last month, Sahithi's third and final WGM norm came at the IM VII Round Robin in Serbia. The 2007-born player finished second with 6/9, recorded a performance rating of 2408, and gained 23 rating points. That completed the requirements.The first two norms came in Hungary. The first was achieved at the Golden Horse IM Round Robin in September 2025, while the second came at the Kanizsa Open in August 2026, where she defeated GM Yeshaayahu Tzidkiya and recorded a performance rating of 2429.On paper, it may look like a clean progression. But the story behind it is much messier.To give a glimpse of how challenging it has been, when Sahithi was six, she caught dengue. She was on a ventilator for a week. She survived, and her family has always seen her recovery as a second life.Long before chess became a part of his life, Lokeswara Moogi Rao, also known as Lokesh in the circuit, had discovered his passion in literature. During his college days, he spent hours immersed in English novels and occasionally tried his hand at writing. Years later, that love for literature would find its way into the name of his second daughter.“Sahithi is similar to Sahitya, which means literature,” Lokesh explained. But the name had another influence, one rooted in music.Lokesh comes from a family with a rich artistic background. His father’s side of the family was involved in theatre, and music was also part of their household. Lokesh himself was a keen singer, winning several prizes at the state level. Among the ragas he particularly admired was Amruthavarshini, whose name he wanted to draw upon for his daughter.His wife, however, felt that literature deserved a place in the name, too. And so, the two influences came together — Sahithi, inspired by literature, and Varshini, drawn from music.“But eventually, she didn’t belong to either of the two and chose the 64 squares,” Lokesh said with a smile. “She made a name for herself in a different domain.”Lokesh was born in a remote village on the edge of Yarada Hills, close enough to the sea that you could see it from the top. But there was no electricity. Before his father secured a job, the family had depended on fishing for a livelihood, as generations on his father’s side had done in a village near Srikakulam district. Walking to the next colony for food took half an hour.He still became a school topper and then a state-ranked student in the engineering entrance. But the family could not afford it. Lokesh's father had retired, and there was no financial backup. He left the course, took a small job after completing a diploma course, and finished an engineering degree by correspondence. Years later, he joined HPCL as an officer.Lokesh was in his early 30s when he started taking chess seriously. He ran a literature club, a small group that exchanged idioms, short stories, and poems by email, trying to sharpen their English in Vizag.One member, Dinesh, a young medical student who lived opposite him, brought a huge chess trophy to the club one day after becoming the Andhra University chess champion. Having learnt that Lokesh had played chess as a child, Dinesh turned up at his house at ten one night with a chessboard.Lokesh's wife Jaya Sri, however, was left unimpressed, asking the two of them to play the game on the balcony.Lokesh was close to winning the first game and then collapsed. The next day Dinesh won two more. The day after, he won two again, and told Lokesh he had found his weakness. "I took it as a challenge," Lokesh recalled. "I wanted to win one game against him. That is how it started."He bought a book from a local shop and began reading in the refinery's control room, where officers sit around digital boards operating the plant. He would sketch positions on paper, then rub them out and redraw. A senior colleague, VS Prasad, caught him doing it and asked if he played chess. Lokesh begged him not to tell the bosses. Prasad took him home instead, to a shelf of 40 or 50 chess books.One was Max Euwe's The Road to Chess Mastery. For a man in love with literature, it certainly felt like a heaven. "It was like a Sherlock Holmes novel kind of a thing," he told this website.Soon, beating Dinesh became a routine. "I won some five to ten games straight away," he shared.Within three months, he made the HPCL team, and within six months of that he was at the national selections for the Petroleum Sports Promotion Board (PSPB), finishing second. He played for the board for roughly seven years, often captaining HPCL.At tournaments, he shared the hall with grandmasters such as Pentala Harikrishna, Shyam Sundar and Koneru Humpy, among others.He was never the strongest player in those rooms. Nevertheless, what he had was an appetite for classical chess. He would take an opening idea from a book, set up the position, and put it to the GMs. They told him he would one day be one of the finest coaches in the country."So that was the foundation," he said, giving us a touch of the philosophy behind Sahithi's approach today.The formal coach within Lokesh became active when her daughters started playing. Despite Sahithi showing early promise, he never set himself a target of IM or GM. What he wanted was a particular kind of game."I always had a very big dream to make her someone like Fischer and Kasparov, not a GM and all," he noted. "I never thought of making IM, GM and then celebrate it. Those moments are important, definitely, in life to cherish and move forward. But my dream was to make her someone like a legend."That ambition shows in how she plays. She goes for sacrifices and attacking positions, and her games grabbed early attention.At 14, she was rated over 2200. Her attacking play drew praise from Scottish Grandmaster, world-famous chess trainer, and author Jacob Aagaard. She also beat women's world champion Mariya Muzychuk."She never fears the opponent. She just plays her style," her coach said.Soon, she had also won a stack of age-group medals, among them Asian and Commonwealth golds.Then came COVID. Sahithi was at her peak, rated highly and seeded at the top of her age groups, and the tournaments stopped. She missed almost three years of competitive chess."You are playing so well, and suddenly, you don't have the option of playing continuously," Lokesh said. "That was really annoying."Leave from work was a problem even before the pandemic. She qualified for a world youth championship (the Cadets tournament) but could not travel. After the lockdowns, Lokesh took long leave and moved the family abroad, reasoning that a rented apartment would cost less than repeated flights. It was a gamble, and he knew it.It also exposed a different problem. Online chess meant every game she played in open tournaments was published, and opponents could prepare against her at the click of a button. A player who loved to surprise people was suddenly easy to study. She tried switching openings from one day to the next, which backfired against stronger opposition.Playing 2300-rated players, he explained, you cannot get away with half-prepared systems. "It did backfire for almost a year," he said.But she came out of it understanding more openings than before. And in 2022 she played at the Chess Olympiad in Chennai, a member of India's C women's team and among the youngest in the squad. "Playing for India is always a special thing," Lokesh told this website.After the Olympiad, the targets slipped away. Sahithi secured a 13th-place finish at the FIDE Women's World Rapid Chess Championship 2023 held in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, which also earned praise from former five-time world champion Viswanathan Anand. She was close to 2300 but not there, and the company could not keep granting leave.The trips abroad were expensive. HPCL contributed around Rs 10 lakh to Sahithi's career, and the Andhra Pradesh government gave a similar amount, but it was not enough."I had to sell an apartment," Lokesh revealed. His wife's gold was pledged. He was running out of options when he reached the most difficult decision almost three years back. "There was only one way. I had to quit my job," he recalled.He resigned and set up a chess academy, which he admits was harder than it sounded. A start in Hyderabad did not work for about ten months, partly because he was away at tournaments with Sahithi.Then, following a heart attack, he had a bypass operation, the heart surgery that forced him to stop for months and reduced both his income and his strength.Around the same time, relatives pressed him to make Sahithi finish class 10. She took nine months away from chess to do it."It sets the morale down," he said of the surgery. "Financially, it also consumes."Jaya Sri was a rock throughout. "I appreciate my wife more than me to be more braver than myself," he said. For a woman who was not earning and had no connection to chess, living with selling property, shifting country, and watching her husband leave his job, he considers it a far harder act of faith than his own.His elder daughter Falguni, now a FIDE arbiter, helped too, paying her own fees and rent by teaching classes.The decision to open the chess academy turned out better than he feared. Back in Visakhapatnam, the academy grew.His student Ajay santhosh Parvathareddy has amassed two GM norms and is now on the verge of beocoming a grand master. Aarav Sinha has collected four IM norms, and others gained hundreds of rating points within months on the European circuit. More than fifteen players now train with him, and he is writing a book on the 2200 level."After surgery, I have had bigger achievements compared to pre-surgery," he remarked.Sahithi was his first student. She remains the one he measures the rest against. But she is not, by his father's account, in the best place mentally."She is a little demotivated, to be frank," Lokesh added. The three lost years still weigh on her. His advice, however, stays the same every time."How you start is not as important as how you end," he tells her. "Whatever you missed in those years, no regrets for that. Just look at what opportunities you have."The plan is to build strength rather than chase a rating. "If you are 2500, you should be able to play like a 2500," he explained. "It should not merely happen with your rating. You should deserve it."The harder obstacle is access. Official events such as the Asian Championships, Commonwealth events and World Juniors come with hotel costs that the family cannot easily meet. Lokesh believes that if Sahithi is given those platforms, results and sponsors will follow. If not, he will keep creating his own opportunities."I'm optimistic that way, rather than regretting not having big sponsors," he acknowledged, thanking Pravaha Foundation for currently sponsoring the chess prodigy in her journey."There are no big names in this journey. No godfathers. You don't require big names to make your stamp. It is your willpower, your passion for the game, your determination, and how you sustain in the difficult phases that take you forward."Perhaps Sagar Shah had got it right all those years ago. Like rice that takes time to cook to perfection over a gentle flame, Sahithi Varshini, too, may need time to come into her own. And when she does, it may well be to carry forward the legacy of those who came before her in chess, sooner rather than later.
Article Summary: Vizag-born prodigy Sahithi Varshini recently became India’s latest Woman Grandmaster (WGM) Her father Lokeswara Moogi Rao, her only coach to date, tells TimesofIndia.com: "This is just a mere beginning"

Former Australia captain Steve Smith has been cleared of concussion and resumed fielding duties on the fifth day of the first Test against South Africa at Kingsmead in Durban on Tuesday, after undergoing a series of clinical assessments following a blow to the helmet.The 37-year-old batter was struck by a short-pitched delivery from Anrich Nortje during Australia's second innings. Smith attempted to duck under the ball but misjudged its trajectory as it failed to rise as much as he expected.Although he continued batting after the incident, scoring 27 off 41 balls before being caught at long-on off Simon Harmer, Smith did not take the field when South Africa began their second innings on Monday. Michael Neser served as his substitute fielder during that session.However, Smith returned to the field on Tuesday morning after being cleared under Cricket Australia's concussion protocols. He was stationed in the slip cordon when South Africa resumed their chase and subsequently took a catch to dismiss Kyle Verreynne off Matt Renshaw's bowling."Steve Smith has undergone a series of clinical assessments over the past 24 hours in accordance with Cricket Australia’s concussion protocols and has been cleared to take the field this morning," Cricket Australia said in a statement.The incident brought back memories of Smith's previous concussion scare during the 2019 Ashes in England, when he was struck on the head by fast bowler Jofra Archer and forced to miss part of a Test match.Smith's return to the field came after medical assessments over the preceding 24 hours, with Australia following the prescribed protocols before allowing the experienced batter to resume his duties.His presence was a boost for Australia as they pushed for victory in the series opener, with South Africa mounting a determined resistance on the final day.South Africa resumed at 102/4 on Tuesday, needing another 319 runs to win. They reached 166/6 by lunch after Australia struck twice to strengthen their grip on the contest.Opener Aiden Markram led the home side's resistance, remaining unbeaten on 69 at the interval alongside Marco Jansen on seven. The pair had to rebuild after Wiaan Mulder's patient 69-run fifth-wicket partnership with Markram ended when Josh Hazlewood had Mulder caught behind by Alex Carey.Part-time spinner Matt Renshaw then dismissed Verreynne, who made just one before edging a reckless shot to Smith at slip.Renshaw has been Australia's standout performer with the bat, having scored 190 in the first innings and 82 in the second, before adding two wickets to his match contribution.Australia needed four more wickets at lunch to seal victory in the opening Test. The second Test of the series is scheduled to begin in Gqeberha on Sunday.
Article Summary: Steve Smith cleared of concussion after blow to the helmet. Former Australia captain was struck by short-pitched delivery from Anrich Nortje. Smith took a catch to dismiss Kyle Verreynne off Matt Renshaw's bowling. Australia needed four more wickets at lunch to seal victory in the opening Test.

Article Title: Ranji Trophy: Mahipal Lomror holds firm to help Rajasthan earn 3 points against Tamil Nadu
Article Text:
Mahipal Lomror (Image credit: BCCI Domestic)

JAIPUR: Mahipal Lomror scored a gritty 84 that helped Rajasthan secure three vital points against Tamil Nadu as the four-day Ranji Trophy Elite Group D match ended in a tame draw at the Sawai Mansingh Stadium here on Wednesday. TN had to be happy with one point after they had conceded the 89-run first-innings lead on Tuesday.Tamil Nadu needed a few quick wickets in the first session on Day 4 to give themselves a chance for victory but Mahipal and Kartik Sharma shattered their hopes with a solid 78-run stand for the fourth wicket. Extending their stay from 81/4 on Day 3, Mahipal and Kartik not only denied the visitors any wicket but also scored at a fairly quick pace to take the game beyond their reach.By the time, Kartik (42: 75b, 4x4, 2x6) got out trying to sweep Sai Kishore for another boundary, the hosts were more or less in a safe zone. Ajay Singh Kukna then frustrated the opponents by providing solid support to Mahipal.Mahipal’s second half-century of the match and his 83-run stand for the sixth wicket with Kukna (32*: 79b, 3x4) closed the door on TN’s comeback bid. After Mahipal was finally dismissed for 84 (170b, 7x4), Manav Suthar declared the innings giving an impossible-looking target of 282 in less than two sessions.The visitors did not make any effort to chase and settled for some batting practice reaching 73/0 at tea break. Sai Sudharsan, who got out for just 3 in the first innings, remained unbeaten on 26, while fellow opener Narayan Jagadeesan made 45 not out, when the match was called off.TN skipper Sai Kishore and newly-appointed coach Yo Mahesh did not seem too disappointed with the result.“There are several positives from this season-opener. Deepesh Devendran impressed with his three-wicket haul on debut. Experienced seamer Saravana Kumar also made a strong comeback, while Andre Siddharth batted brilliantly to keep our hopes alive on the third day. Sai Kishore gave us early breakthroughs in the second essay,” Yo Mahesh said.Sai Kishore felt the lower-order collapse put them on the backfoot. “We had a fairly good start with both Jagadeesan and Pradosh hitting fifties. Then Baba Indrajith and Andre kept us in the hunt but once that unfortunate run out of Sonu Yadav happened it did affect our march towards taking the first-innings lead. Rajasthan bowlers especially Kukna bowled really well,” said Sai Kishore.Yo Mahesh rued the fact that they couldn’t make use of their chances.“We had our chances but we couldn’t latch on to those. In the second innings we had Rajasthan reeling at 31/4 and we should have capitalised on it. Credit must be given to Mahipal and Kartik for the way they batted and frustrated us. The toss, too, played a critical role,” said Yo Mahesh.Manav was pleased with the result and lauded his young team for getting the better of their strong opponents."Certainly it was a very good result for us. Tamil Nadu is traditionally a formidable side with a couple of India players in their ranks. We did really well to start with three points. It's a positive beginning for us in the season," Manav told TOI after the match.Three players -- Rohan Rajbhar, Chetan Sharma and Hemant Kumar -- made their debut for Rajasthan, who also missed the services of regular bowlers like Khaleel Ahmed, Aniket Choudhary, Deepak Chahar and Rahul Chahar."We went into the match with an inexperienced side but debutants Rohan and Chetan did remarkably well. Even Karan Lamba returned to the side after two years and struck an important hundred. Kukna's five-wicket haul turned the match in our favour and Mahipal batted well in both the innings. Overall it was almost a perfect start for us," said Manav, who will leave for New Zealand in a couple of days to join India 'A' side.BRIEF SCORESRajasthan 363 and 192/6 declared in 34 overs (Mahipal Lomror 84, Kartik Sharma 42, Ajay Singh Kukna 32*; Sai Kishore 3-50 ). Tamil Nadu 274 and 73/0 in 98.4 overs (Sai Sudharsan 26*, Narayan Jagadeesan 45*) Match drawn.Points: Rajasthan 3; TN 1.
Article Summary: Mahipal Lomror scores 84 as Rajasthan secure three vital points against Tamil Nadu. The four-day Ranji Trophy Elite Group D match ended in a tame draw on Wednesday. Tamil Nadu had to be happy with one point after they had conceded the 89-run first-innings lead on Tuesday.

Article Title: IND vs NZ: Can New Zealand stop India's big hitters? Mitchell Santner reveals his plan
Article Text:
Abhishek Sharma and Mitchell Santner (Image credit: Agencies)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Poll Vote & Share your view Will New Zealand successfully manage the aggressive Indian batting lineup? Yes, definitely! Maybe, depends on the conditions! No, it's too tough! 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

New Zealand white-ball captain Mitchell Santner is under no illusions about the challenge that awaits his side against India’s explosive top order. With the likes of Abhishek Sharma, Ishan Kishan and Sanju Samson capable of dismantling bowling attacks from the outset, Santner knows the Black Caps will need more than discipline to keep the visitors in check.As New Zealand prepare for the five-match T20I series, the left-arm spinner is hoping the early-season conditions offer some assistance, while stressing the need for his bowlers to adapt quickly and stay in the contest even when the boundaries begin to flow.“ They pack power all the way through and come out with a lot of aggression. As a bowler, you know there aren’t going to be too many dot balls. You have to plan accordingly, assess the conditions and use them to your advantage,” Santner said.The New Zealand captain acknowledged that boundaries would inevitably come against such an aggressive opposition, but stressed that bowlers must focus on the deliveries between them.“Even if you get hit for boundaries, it is about what happens with the balls in between. Those could be wicket-taking deliveries or dot balls. If we can restrict India to around 200 in New Zealand, that might be a good score, considering the power they possess,” he added.The prospect of facing Abhishek, Ishan and Sanju has prompted Santner to emphasise tactical flexibility, particularly during the powerplay. The early-season pitches in Christchurch could offer movement.“If the ball moves, we need to use that to counter their explosive batting. But if the pitch is flat, then we might have to create pressure, by using the bigger boundaries and finding different ways of taking wickets,” he said.Santner acknowledged that the power-packed nature of modern T20 cricket has made life increasingly difficult for bowlers, with even conceding 30-40 runs in a spell potentially representing a good performance.“If you can take two or three wickets for around 30 or even under 40 runs, you are probably doing a very good job. Against someone like Abhishek or Ishan, you know they will come hard from ball one. You have to decide whether that means bowling yorkers, arm balls or taking the ball away from their hitting arc,” he explained.Santner also acknowledged the threat posed by young sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi. Having seen the teenager’s exploits in the IPL, the New Zealand captain expects India’s power-hitters to test his bowlers from the outset.“I’ve seen what he can do at the IPL. Whether it is Sooryavanshi, Abhishek, Ishan or Sanju, India have power throughout the lineup. It will be a challenge to stop him.”Santner also acknowledged that India could arrive with a point to prove following New Zealand’s historic 3-0 Test series triumph on Indian soil and a 2-1 ODI series victory.“You never like losing a series at home. The more you play in places like India, the better equipped you become to handle the conditions. India might have a point to prove, but our job is to play what is in front of us and beat a very good team at home,” he said.With Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma continuing to attract enormous attention for the ODIs, Santner expects the tour to bring its share of excitement.“Rohit and Kohli may not be getting any younger, but they are still churning out the runs.”
Article Summary: Mitchell Santner under no illusions about the challenge that awaits his side against India’s explosive top order. Santner: “They pack power all the way through and come out with a lot of aggression. As a bowler, you know there aren’t going to be too many dot balls. You have to plan accordingly, assess the conditions and use them to your advantage”

Article Title: BCCI raises selectors' budget by Rs 5 cr as hunt for Ajit Agarkar's replacement continues
Article Text:
Pragyan Ojha (Image credit: X)

VVS to have bigger say?

Board willing to increase budget to rope in big names

Will SS Das continue after Dec?

NEW DELHI: There’s ambiguity around the composition of the BCCI ’s national selection committee following former chief Ajit Agarkar’s decision not to continue. The deadline for applications to fill the West Zone vacancy ended on Wednesday with former India wicketkeeper Parthiv Patel , who was widely tipped to be Agarkar’s replacement, choosing not to apply for the job.Parthiv’s decision to opt out has given rise to speculation that the head of the BCCI’s Centre of Excellence (CoE), VVS Laxman , may have a greater say in selection affairs, with Pragyan Ojha continuing as the interim chairman of the selection committee. With the ODI World Cup less than a year away, will the BCCI choose to continue with the two?“BCCI would have preferred continuity with Agarkar staying on till the World Cup, but things didn’t go as expected. If a new chairman of selection committee comes in, there’s a chance his vision could be different from the ones working now. So, the board will have to gauge the vision of the new selector,” a BCCI source said, adding, “With Laxman’s growing influence, the board may let things remain the way they are at present. ”It will be interesting to see if the board takes more time to find a suitable candidate for the chief selector’s role.Or else, it is likely it will proceed with candidates to just fill up the spot for a representative from the west zone.According to sources, the BCCI prefers ‘big’ names with a considerable amount of international cricket behind them to take up important positions. TOI has learnt that the board has become flexible in its pay policy to rope in the big names.Since RP Singh and Pragyan Ojha joined the selection committee in Sept last year, BCCI’s expenses on selection committees exceeded the annual budget by Rs 3 crore to Rs 17.45 crore. Interestingly, the board has reserved a budget of Rs 19.35 cr for 2026-27, marking an increase of another Rs 2 cr. That implies BCCI has increased the budget for the selection committees by Rs 5 cr.TOI understands that the board had reached out to a couple of former cricketers who have played close to 100 Tests, but they declined the offer. It is learnt that recent appointments in the men’s selection committee have happened with candidates negotiating their salaries.The BCCI has to also deliberate if it wants to continue with SS Das as a selector since he will complete four years in the job in Dec. Sources said that there’s a chance that the board will let Das continue till the World Cup.
Article Summary: The deadline for applications to fill the West Zone vacancy ended on Wednesday. Former India wicketkeeper Parthiv Patel chose not to apply for the job. VVS Laxman may have a greater say in selection affairs, with Pragyan Ojha continuing as the interim chairman of the selection committee.

HYDERABAD: Captain Shai Hope continued his dream run, scoring his second century of the T20I series - an unbeaten 102 (50b; 4x4, 9x6) - while pacer Keemo Paul bagged 5/41 as the West Indies defeated India by 24 runs to make it 2-2 and keep the fivematch series alive here at the Rajiv Gandhi International stadium on Wednesday.After the West Indies were put in to bat, Hope hit his third century in T20Is to power the visitors to 247/3. Later, Paul’s exploits on a batter-friendly wicket saw India finish at 223 in 19.3 overs as last batter Arshdeep retired hurt.Chasing a stiff target, Samson (56; 23b, 6x4, 4x6) launched into Shamar Joseph with consecutive sixes and Roston Chase with two boundaries and as many sixes to take India to 50 in three overs. He reached his half-century off just 20 balls while Abhishek Sharma played just three deliveries at the other end in that period. However, Samson departed after pulling Paul straight into the hands of Hetmyer at deep square leg.Ishan Kishan (6) also holed out to deep midwicket as the hosts went to 80/2 in the Powerplay. Captain Shreyas Iyer sliced Shamar Springer to backward point, reducing India to 97/3 in 8.2 overs.At the halfway stage, they were 115/3, needing 133 more for victory.However, Gudakesh Motie derailed the chase by striking twin blows in the 12th over. He first ended Abhishek’s uncharacteristic 29 (24b; 3x4, 1x6) as the batter holed out to longoff, followed by Naman Dhir being stumped first ball.Tilak Varma and Nitish Kumar Reddy tried to keep their side in the hunt. Nitish took a special liking to Shamar Joseph, hitting him for 21 runs with a boundary and consecutive sixes in the 16th over to bring down the equation to 53 from five overs. However, Tilak (43; 25b, 2x4, 3x6) was caught at mid-off off Shepherd that reduced India to 200/6.There on, the chase proved too steep for the hosts. Paul removed Nitish (41; 20b, 1x4, 4x6), Prince Yadav and Axar Patel in four deliveries of the 19th over.Earlier, Jewel Andrew and Hope provided a quick start, putting 50 runs on the board in just 3.3 overs. Axar provided the breakthrough, dismissing Andrew (21; 16b, 2x4, 1x6) by trapping him in front. But Hetmyer maintained the momentum to take his side to 79/1 in the Powerplay.Prince removed Hetmyer (33; 12b, 4x4, 2x6) and at the half-way stage, West Indies were 118/2. Hope lofted Mayank for a six to reach his half-century in 28 balls.Arshdeep got rid of Rovman Powell (24; 17b, 2x4, 1x6) in the 13th over, but Sherfane Rutherford (49*; 26b, 4x4, 3x6) and Hope added an unbroken 91 runs in 43 deliveries to provide the final flourish. Hope, needing 10 runs of the innings’ final two deliveries for his century, hit Reddy for two sixes to reach the three-figure mark.

West Indies captain Shai Hope reflected on his outstanding form after leading his team to a 24-run victory over India in the fourth T20I. His unbeaten century helped West Indies level the five-match series 2-2, setting up a decisive final match in Bengaluru on October 17. Hope has enjoyed a remarkable tour of India, collecting three Player of the Match awards so far.Hope joked about the difficulty of carrying his growing collection of awards back home, while stressing that his main goal is to help the team win."To be honest, those (POTM trophies) were a bit heavy; we got to look at luggage weight. NEW DELHI: Para cycling chief coach Aditya Mehta on Wednesday withdrew from the Indian contingent for the Aichi-Nagoya Para Asian Games in protest after eligible cyclists were denied selection. Arshad Shaik is now the lone cyclist to travel to Japan, with only a technician for support.Mehta, who has spent 13 years developing Indian para cycling, said he could not abandon athletes whose “hard-earned opportunities have been taken away”. Mehta will stay back in India while sending Shaik with technician Ramesh Pandi, along with the necessary equipment and technical guidance.“I need to stand by my other athletes, who have worked equally hard but have been denied their opportunity to compete at the Games,” Mehta told TOI, warning that the decision could jeopardise India’s Los Angeles Paralympic qualification prospects.He said India’s Asian rankings — seventh in the men’s category and fourth in the women’s — underline the importance of competing and accumulating points at crucial international events. The actual impact on qualification will depend on the applicable rules and final slot allocation.In a late reprieve, the sports ministry approved two Boccia athletes, Sachin Chamaria and Anjali Devi, for the individual events after initially withholding clearance.Their inclusion takes India’s athlete strength to 168, with 112 men and 56 women competing across 11 disciplines. The overall contingent now stands at 281, including 113 officials.India’s para athletes have also been hit by delayed clearances, triggering a logistical scramble with direct flights to Nagoya no longer available and fares reportedly soaring to five times their usual levels.Athletes now are flying to Tokyo before undertaking a roughly four-hour bus journey to Nagoya, TOIhas learnt. The late bookings leave little time for recovery after the long journey, with some events beginning on Friday.
Article Summary: Para cycling chief coach Aditya Mehta withdraws from the Indian contingent for the Aichi-Nagoya Para Asian Games in protest. Arshad Shaik is now the lone cyclist to travel to Japan, with only a technician for support. Boccia gets last-minute clearance for individual events.

I did the required exercises and it’s fine now. I am confident of achieving my personal best,” said the Paris Paralympics bronze medallist.While he may not have had the smoothest build-up to the Games, 2026 has still been a memorable year for Hokato. The 42-year-old became world No. 1 in his category and also set a national record with a massive throw of 15.21m at the Indian Open Para Athletics Championships in Bengaluru.But Hokato knows that if he is to stand atop the podium, he may have to get past a familiar face: Soman Rana.Ranked world No. 3, 43-year-old Soman Rana arrives at the Asian Para Games as the reigning Commonwealth Games champion and a two-time World Championships silver medallist, having finished runner-up in 2024 and 2025.The pair have trained together at the Army Paralympic Node in Pune since 2017 under coach Rakesh Rawat, developing both a strong friendship and a fierce rivalry.“We’re very close friends. We eat together, train together and spend a lot of time together. Our coordination is excellent,” said Soman, who suffered a mine blast injury while serving with the 2/8 Gorkha Rifles along the Line of Control in Jammu & Kashmir on Dec 1, 2006.For Hokato that friendship comes with an added competitive edge. “There is definitely a lot of competitiveness. We train together and help each other improve, but once competition starts, everyone wants to win,” he said.Rawat believes that rivalry has been one of the biggest reasons behind their development on the international stage.“They motivate each other a great deal,” Rawat said. “Training together gives them valuable experience. They are friends and support each other, but once competition begins, friendship takes a back seat and they become rivals. The one who performs best on the day wins.”The coach expects both throwers to be in contention for medals and insists there is little to separate them. “The rivalry between them has helped both improve. They are very closely matched. On the day, it could go either way,” he said.Soman agrees, although his Commonwealth Games gold is likely to provide an added boost. “The gold gave me a lot of confidence. But I’ve been in this sport for many years. My confidence was already there and winning the medal only strengthened it,” he said.While both athletes believe a podium finish is within reach, neither is willing to predict who will come out on top.For Hokato, however, a gold medal would carry special significance. Since winning bronze in Paris, the road has not been easy. His father passed away last Dec, while he has also been overseeing the construction of a house in his village of P. Vihoto in Nagaland and supporting his daughter, who recently began an MBA programme in Pune.On the field, injuries disrupted his season and forced him to miss the World Para Athletics Grand Prix in New Delhi. Yet, despite the setbacks, Hokato has remained focused on recovery and training.“Recovery is crucial. If you don’t recover properly, there’s no point competing. You can travel all that way and still return empty-handed,” he said.Now, he is eager to return to competition and renew his rivalry with Soman on one of para athletics’ biggest stages. For India, it could be an ideal scenario: two close friends pushing each other every day in training before battling for continental glory when it matters most.
Article Summary: Hokato Hotozhe Sema is the world No. 2 shot putter in the F57 category. Soman Rana is the reigning Commonwealth Games champion. The pair have trained together at the Army Paralympic Node in Pune since 2017.

Article Title: Rakesh Nidagundi designs his destiny from graphics to Asian Para Games
Article Text:
Rakesh Nidagundi

PUNE: Destiny works in mysterious ways. With his legs affected by polio since childhood, Hubballi’s Rakesh Nidagundi, thought a career in graphic design, would suit him better.Until 2017, he had no idea that it would only open doors to bigger opportunities and a sporting life that he had never thought of.On Wednesday, the Karnataka shooter, 38, will travel to Japan for the Asian Para Games, his first multi-sport event since he started shooting in 2021.“I am very excited and prepared for the Asian Para Games. I have worked hard for this, and I am hoping to do well,” the rifle shooter told TOI. The Karnataka shooter will participate in the 10m air rifle SH1 category at the Aichi-Nagoya Games.Shooting happened to Rakesh by chance. While at his office, he got an order to design a creative publishing material for a shooting academy in Hubballi. “That was the first time I got to know about shooting. The coach at the academy, Ravichandra Balehosur, asked me to visit his academy and try out the sport," Rakesh, who now trains and is sponsored by the Vijayi Bharat Foundation in Ahmedabad, said.“I didn’t think of trying the sport then, but during the Covid-19 lockdown in 2020, I had no work, so I decided to try it once the lockdown was relaxed.I fell in love with the sport and started competing in 2021,” Rakesh said.After he started competing, his life changed after he won medals at the Khelo India Games. “I was supported by the government through the National Centre of Excellence and VBF also came forward to help me. Since then, I have been improving consistently and have won medals at the World level,” said the shooter, who won silver at the World Shooting Para Sport (WSPS) in Changwon, last month.
Article Summary: Rakesh Nidagundi, 38, will travel to Japan for the Asian Para Games. The Karnataka shooter will participate in the 10m air rifle SH1 category at the Aichi-Nagoya Games. His legs have been affected by polio since childhood.

Article Title: Asian Para Games: Defending champion Shailesh Kumar ready for another big jump
Article Text:
Shailesh Kumar

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

KOLKATA: There was a time when people in his village wondered what future awaited him.Unable to walk properly since childhood after being diagnosed with polio in his right leg, Shailesh Kumar, a resident of Islamnagar village in Bihar’s Jamui district, often faced doubts about what he could achieve.Today, the same people urge him to bring glory to the country, thanks to the success he has achieved in para-athletics. The T63 high jumper heads to the Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, as the defending champion, carrying not just expectations but also the confidence that comes from changing lives, including his own.“Life has changed significantly, both financially and socially. Earlier, people would wonder what I could achieve because I couldn’t walk properly. Today, their mindset has changed. They see that a para athlete can represent the country and achieve success,” Shailesh told TOI ahead of the Games.Since winning gold with a Games record at the 2023 Asian Para Games in China, the 26-year-old has added several major titles to his résumé, including gold medals at 2025 World Para Athletics Championships and 2026 World Para Athletics Grand Prix.Training under close friend and coach Ronak Malik in Bengaluru since Jan 2025, the 26-year-old is now focused on defending his high jump title.He enters the competition after overcoming knee issues that troubled him earlier in the season, but Malik is confident his ward can retain the gold medal in high jump and also contend for a podium finish in long jump.“If everything goes according to plan, he has the potential to win medals in both events. Gold is definitely a possibility. He has already set records at the World Championships and Asian Championships and has achieved personal best performances,” said Malik, a former national-level high jumper.Training a para athlete requires a different approach from coaching able-bodied athletes, and Malik regularly consults experienced jump coach GV Gaonkar to fine-tune Shailesh’s programme.While Malik’s guidance has proved hugely beneficial on the field, their friendship has also played a key role in Shailesh’s resurgence, particularly after Paris Paralympics, where he narrowly missed a medal and finished fourth.“After beginning his training in Sonipat in 2019, Shailesh moved to SAI Gandhinagar under coach Vinod Chauhan. Unfortunately, Vinod sir passed away in a road accident in April 2023. It was a difficult phase for Shailesh and he wasn’t in the best frame of mind going into the Paris Paralympics,” Malik said.It was after Chauhan’s death that Shailesh reconnected with Malik. Together, they are now targeting success not only at the Asian Para Games but also at next year’s World Championships and, ultimately, the Paralympics in LA.But as Malik says, none of it would have been possible without the discipline and dedication of Shailesh, who chose sport even as his family hoped he would focus on studies and secure a stable job.“People had different opinions about me, so I wanted to do something different. My family stood by me throughout and today they are very proud,” said Shailesh.But as he prepares for another Asian Para Games campaign, he remains determined not to be weighed down by expectations. “I am the defending champion, but I am an athlete first. When you represent the country there is pressure, but I try to keep it to a minimum and perform freely,” he said.For Shailesh, though, the biggest motivation remains the journey itself. From being doubted because of his disability to becoming a champion who inspires others, he believes para-sports have given him a life he never imagined, and he intends to make the most of it.
Article Summary: Shailesh Kumar is the defending champion of the T63 high jump at the Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. The 26-year-old was diagnosed with polio in his right leg as a child. He has won several major titles, including gold medals at 2025 World Para Athletics Championships and 2026 World ParA Athletics Grand Prix.

Article Title: Ban threat on para shooters for challenging PCI in court
Article Text:
Imag credit: X

NEW DELHI: With India’s Asian Para Games preparations already marred by selection disputes and court battles, the Paralympic Committee of India (PCI) has landed in another controversy over a para shooting policy that threatens athletes with lengthy bans for challenging its decisions in court.A clause in the PCI governing body-approved 2026-27 national selection policy for para shooting prescribes a three-year ban if a shooter or their parents initiate legal action against the association and the case is dismissed. A repeat offence could invite a lifetime ban, according to the 16-page policy, a copy of which is with TOI.“Any para shooters/coaches/parents going to the courts or taking any legal action against the association and further if the case is dismissed by the court, the para shooter would be banned for at least three years and in case of repeated offence, ban could go for lifetime as well,” the clause states.The provision raises questions about athletes’ right to seek judicial redress in selection disputes, potentially exposing para shooters to severe sporting sanctions for challenging the PCI’s decisions.A senior PCI official told TOI that the clause was damaging and should never have been included. The official said directions had been issued to amend the policy and that a corrigendum would be uploaded. However, since the policy was approved by the governing body, a formal amendment may be necessary.It is learnt that some shooters unhappy with their exclusion from the Asian Para Games squad refrained from approaching the courts for fear of being banned.Boccia dropped, contingent shrinks to 10 sportsThe controversy comes amid further reductions in India’s contingent for the Games. After para fencing, boccia has become the latest discipline to be dropped, with the sports ministry withholding clearance for the two-member team of Sachin Chamaria and Anjali Devi.India, initially scheduled to compete in 12 sports, will now participate in 10. The ministry cleared 166 athletes late Monday evening, taking the delegation’s strength to 275, including 94 team officials and support staff and 15 contingent staff. The Games begin in Nagoya on Oct 18.Para athletics accounts for the largest share of the contingent, with 62 athletes, including 46 men, along with 36 support staff.Para shooting chief coach JP Nautiyal has not received clearance despite representations from nine of the 13 selected shooters. Jeevan L Rai and Rakesh Singh will oversee the team. Nautiyal has faced allegations of violating selection criteria and demanding kickbacks.Cyclists’ hopes end with DRMThe final Delegation Registration Meeting (DRM) in Nagoya on Monday has effectively closed the door on additional entries. Para cyclists awaiting court relief against their exclusion will miss the Games even if they secure a favourable order later.Only Arshad Shaik will compete, while six other cyclists selected by the Cycling Federation of India and the PCI were omitted for allegedly failing to meet the prescribed criteria.Baretha questions Suhas’ inclusionPara badminton player Chirag Baretha has questioned the last-minute inclusion of LY Suhas, citing his absence from national and international competition since the Paris Paralympics in 2024.Baretha, a two-time Asian Para Games medallist, was excluded after the ministry ruled that he did not meet the selection criteria.“How a player can be qualified and sanctioned in the events at the Asian Para Games, he has never played a single game in the events he is qualified. Arbitration in sports can be visibly seen with the sanction issued for upcoming Games,” Baretha wrote on X.Manisha Patel, Shashank Kumar, Ammu Beulah Mohan and Rachna Patel were also denied clearance by the ministry.
Article Summary: PCI threatens athletes with lengthy bans for challenging its decisions in court. Clause in 2026-27 national selection policy for para shooting prescribes three- year ban if a shooter or their parents initiate legal action against the association. A repeat offence could invite a lifetime ban, according to the 16-page policy.

Article Title: Coach axed after explosive selection row! India name 166 athletes for Asian Para Games 2026

Para-badminton player Pramod Bhagat, para-archer Rakesh Kumar, para table tennis player Bhavina Patel, and others during the send-off ceremony. (PTI Photo)
